sections.heading: Present Simple
sections.explanation: Use for habits, permanent states, timetables, scientific facts, instructions and dramatic narration. Form: base verb; add -s/-es for he/she/it. Questions and negatives use do/does. Time clues: usually, often, every day, on Mondays.
examples: He goes swimming every day.
She works in a bank.
The match begins at 8:30 next Monday evening.
Ice melts when heated.
First you chop the meat, then you fry it.
The lights go out and a figure tears out of the villa.

sections.heading: Present Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: am/is/are + -ing. Use for actions happening now, temporary situations, fixed near-future arrangements, changing trends, or repeated annoying actions with always/forever/constantly. Time clues: now, at present, at the moment, these days.
examples: You’re always leaving the cap off the toothpaste.
He’s sleeping at the moment.
They’re hunting for a flat.
They are going on an excursion tomorrow.
Oil prices are rising at present.

sections.heading: Present Perfect
sections.explanation: Form: have/has + past participle. Use for recent completion, experience without a definite past time, results up to now, and situations continuing to the present. Time clues: since, for, yet, already, just, ever, so far, recently.
examples: She has just painted her room.
He has written three books.
She has seen this film.
I’ve been to Berlin twice.
He has worked as a teacher for four years.

sections.heading: Present Perfect Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: have/has been + -ing. Focus on duration or activity continuing to now, present evidence of a past activity, or annoyance. Time clues: for, since, how long, lately, recently. Compare the finished result with the ongoing activity.
examples: She has been painting her room. (It smells of paint.)
She has been waiting for two hours but there’s still no sign of him.
What have you been doing to my computer?

sections.heading: Stative verbs
sections.explanation: Verbs describing senses, thoughts, feelings, possession and appearance normally use simple forms: see, hear, smell, taste; think, believe, doubt; like, hate, love; belong, own, owe, seem. A continuous form can change the meaning to an activity or arrangement.
examples: I’m seeing my dentist tomorrow.
Do you see those birds?
Be quiet, please! I’m thinking.
I think you are wrong.
We were having a good time at the party when the fire broke out.
Since you have his phone number, you can call him.

sections.heading: Been to / been in / gone to
sections.explanation: Been to means visited and returned. Been in describes staying or living somewhere for a period. Gone to means left for a place and has not returned yet.
examples: He has been to Berlin. (= He has gone and come back.)
He has been in Buenos Aires for a year. (= He lives there.)
He has gone to Toledo. (= He hasn’t come back yet.)

sections.heading: Will / shall
sections.explanation: Use will for predictions, offers, promises, requests, spontaneous decisions, and opinions or hopes. Use shall with I/we for offers and suggestions. Form: will + base verb.
examples: Will you help me with the dishes?
Shall I get you some coffee?
“Your clothes are dirty.” “Are they? I’ll wash them.”
I think he’ll pass the test.

sections.heading: Be going to
sections.explanation: Form: am/is/are going to + base verb. Use for intentions, plans, and predictions based on present evidence.
examples: I know my clothes are dirty. I’m going to wash them tomorrow.
She’s going to take her driving test next month.
He doesn’t know how to light a fire. He’s going to burn himself.

sections.heading: Future Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: will be + -ing. Use for an action in progress at a future time, an assumption about what someone is doing now, or a previously planned action.
examples: I’ll be flying to Paris this time tomorrow.
He will be sleeping now. (It’s midnight.)
I’ll be seeing Sam tonight. Would you like me to tell him the news?

sections.heading: Future Perfect
sections.explanation: Form: will have + past participle. Use for completion before a future point and assumptions about completed actions. By/before are common in affirmative sentences; until is used in negative sentences.
examples: By the end of July he will have been in Athens for two months.
He will have gone to sleep by now.
She will have cleaned the house by 6 o’clock.
She won’t have cleaned the house until 6 o’clock.

sections.heading: Future Perfect Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: will have been + -ing. Emphasise duration continuing up to a future point, often with by … for.
examples: By next Sunday, they will have been living here for two weeks.

sections.heading: Other future expressions
sections.explanation: Be + to-infinitive expresses plans or instructions. Be about to + infinitive and be on the point of + -ing express the immediate future.
examples: The meeting is to take place on Wednesday.
You are not to leave the premises until 17:00.
They are about to leave.
They are on the point of leaving.

sections.heading: Past Simple
sections.explanation: Use for completed past actions, sequential events, past habits and events that will not recur. Form: past verb; did + base verb for questions and negatives. Clues: yesterday, ago, last week, when.
examples: He left an hour ago.
She phoned before the boss came.
He travelled/used to travel a lot when he was young.
He stood up, picked up his briefcase and left the office.
Marilyn Monroe starred in “The Seven Year Itch”.

sections.heading: Past Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: was/were + -ing. Use for actions in progress at a past time, background interrupted by another action, simultaneous activities, and polite enquiries.
examples: She was still working at eight o’clock yesterday evening.
She was leaving when the phone rang.
While Jane was getting dressed, Tom was enjoying his drink.
I was wondering if you could help me.

sections.heading: Past Perfect
sections.explanation: Form: had + past participle. It places one event before another past event and acts as the past equivalent of the Present Perfect.
examples: She had already typed all the letters before her boss arrived.
Bob had always dreamed of being in a musical, but he never got the chance.
Tom has always dreamed of being in a musical; he might make it one day.

sections.heading: Past Perfect Continuous
sections.explanation: Form: had been + -ing. Use for a longer activity continuing up to another past event or with visible results at that past time.
examples: She had been cooking all day long when Tom came home with some fish and chips.
She was covered in paint because she had been painting her room.

sections.heading: Used to / be used to / get used to / would
sections.explanation: Used to + infinitive describes a former habit or state. Be/get used to + noun or -ing means be/become accustomed to something. Would describes repeated past actions and routines, rather than past states.
examples: This theatre used to be a hospital.
He used to work till late at night.
She isn’t used to driving on the left.
I haven’t got used to living abroad yet.
When I was at my grandparents’ cottage, I would wake up early and go for a ride.

sections.heading: Superlatives
sections.explanation: Compare never before with the nicest/best … ever.
examples: I’ve never been given such a nice present before.
It’s the nicest present I’ve ever been given.

sections.heading: First experience
sections.explanation: It’s the first time + present perfect.
examples: He’s never flown before.
It’s the first time he’s (ever) flown.

sections.heading: Since and for
sections.explanation: Since names a starting point; for names a duration.
examples: It’s/It’s been a long time since he visited us.
He hasn’t visited us for a long time.

sections.heading: Asking about elapsed time
sections.explanation: How long ago …? / How long is it since …?
examples: When did you leave school?
How long ago did you leave school?
How long is it since you left school?

sections.heading: Last time
sections.explanation: Convert last time + past to a negative present perfect.
examples: The last time I saw her was a month ago.
I haven’t seen her for a month.

sections.heading: Membership
sections.explanation: Starting membership becomes a continuing state.
examples: He joined the golf club ten months ago.
He has been a member of the golf club for ten months.

sections.heading: A month since
sections.explanation: A month since … corresponds to a month ago.
examples: It’s a month since she moved to Austria.
She moved to Austria a month ago.

sections.heading: Continuing lessons
sections.explanation: Present perfect continuous focuses on the activity.
examples: She started English lessons a year ago.
She has been taking/having English lessons for a year.
It’s a year since she started taking/having English lessons.

sections.heading: Earlier completion
sections.explanation: Having + past participle and after + past perfect show sequence.
examples: Having had dinner, I went to bed.
After having dinner, I went to bed.
After I had had dinner, I went to bed.

sections.heading: Prediction
sections.explanation: Expressions of opinion can introduce a prediction.
examples: I think there will be a war soon.
In my opinion, there is going to be a war soon.
If you ask me, there’s bound to be a war soon.
In my estimation, war is imminent.

sections.heading: Belief
sections.explanation: Negative beliefs can be reworded.
examples: I don’t believe that he’ll agree.
It’s my belief that he won’t agree.
I have a feeling that he won’t agree.
There’s no reason to believe that he’ll agree.

sections.heading: While / when
sections.explanation: A time clause can be shortened or emphasised with a cleft.
examples: While I was walking down the street, I saw Mary.
While walking down the street, I saw Mary.
When I was walking down the street, I saw Mary.
It was while I was walking down the street that I saw Mary.

sections.heading: Response / respond
sections.explanation: A noun phrase can become a verb phrase.
examples: Was there any response to his appeal?
Did anyone respond to his appeal?

sections.heading: Scheduled events
sections.explanation: Use take place, be held, or be scheduled.
examples: The race takes place tomorrow.
The race will/is going to be held/take place tomorrow.
The race is scheduled to take place/for tomorrow.

sections.heading: Not until
sections.explanation: Not until at the start requires inversion in the main clause.
examples: She started doing her homework as soon as her brother had left for school.
She started doing her homework when her brother had left for school.
She didn’t start (doing) her homework until her brother had left for school.
She waited until her brother had left for school before she started (doing) her homework.
Not until her brother had left for school did she start (doing) her homework.

sections.heading: Last haircut
sections.explanation: When did you last …? / When was the last time …?
examples: When did you last have a haircut?
When was the last time you had a haircut?

sections.heading: While / during
sections.explanation: While introduces a clause; during introduces a noun phrase.
examples: She wrote the book while she was on holiday.
She wrote the book during her holiday.

sections.heading: Duration as a noun
sections.explanation: An hour’s sleep expresses a duration.
examples: I only slept for an hour last night.
I only had an hour’s sleep last night.

sections.heading: Certainty
sections.explanation: Bound to and no doubt express certainty.
examples: It is certain that he’ll pass his exams.
There is no doubt that he’ll pass his exams.
He is bound to pass his exams.
